db_evidence.notes: episodes table 30sec granularity rows 157278-158418 clearly and explicitly narrate: streamer exits vehicle at 157548s ('steps out of a vehicle onto the sidewalk'), walks past a bakery/market discussing dumplings/sushi at 157758-157848 (without eating), enters a KFC at 157908-157998 ('marvels this is his first time trying kfc in china'), orders a chicken drumstick at 158028s, and takes his first bite at 158208-158238s ('holding a piece of fried chicken... he bites the food'). This matches total_intervals [157748,158314] exactly and matches the reference answer. The DB also contains a separate, unrelated later episode (~160818-161240s) where the streamer exits a car again and eats a dumpling at a food market -- this is a second, later 'getting off' event on the same Shanghai trip, not the first one.

root_causes: rollout-02 anchored on the top-ranked semantic_search hit for 'gets off transportation in Shanghai' (episode starting 160878s) instead of verifying it was chronologically the FIRST such event on the trip; semantic similarity ranked a narratively richer/later 'steps out of car' episode above the earlier, textually plainer one.

Having anchored wrong, rollout-02 then scoped its run_sql window tightly around that anchor (160700-162500), which structurally excluded the true earliest window (157278-158400) from ever being seen, so no later step could self-correct the mistake.
clip_qa in rollout-02 was used only to verify the (wrong) candidate interval it already had, not to check for competing/earlier candidates, so it could not catch the ordering error.
what_worked: Successful rollouts widened the SQL window to span the full candidate arrival period (roughly 157278 to 161200-161500s) rather than trusting a single semantic_search top hit, which surfaced both the early KFC scene and the later dumpling scene for direct chronological comparison.

Rollout-01 recovered from two initially wrong SQL windows (193000-199500 and 296500-301500) by re-running semantic_search and eventually querying the correct range -- persistence/backtracking rescued an initially bad anchor.

Text evidence alone (episodes table) was sufficiently explicit ('first time trying kfc in china', 'orders a chicken drumstick', 'bites the food') that some rollouts (4) could answer correctly without any clip_qa call.
transferable_lessons: For 'first X after Y' questions, do not accept the single highest-ranked semantic_search hit as the anchor event; when multiple candidate 'Y' events exist (e.g. multiple 'gets off vehicle' moments), query a SQL window wide enough to cover the earliest plausible candidate and compare timestamps explicitly.

When narrowing a SQL time window after semantic search, favor widening rather than tightly bracketing the top hit, especially for temporal/ordering questions -- a tight window can permanently hide an earlier competing candidate.
Use clip_qa (or at least a broader run_sql) to check for competing/earlier occurrences of the anchor event, not just to verify the content of the interval already selected.
